result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.find_cliques()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find all maximal cliques in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L9750-L9838){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.find_cliques() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Clique](/assets/graphs/algo-clique.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A six-node graph containing a K4 clique: four mutually connected nodes shown in the accent color, with two extra nodes connected to the clique through default-styled edges." width="100%"} A clique is a subset of nodes where every pair of nodes is connected by an edge. A maximal clique is a clique that cannot be extended by adding another node. Uses the Bron-Kerbosch algorithm for efficient enumeration. Note that this finds *maximal* cliques (cannot be extended), not necessarily *maximum* cliques (largest possible). Use `max_clique()` to find a maximum clique. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of cliques, where each clique is a sorted list of node IDs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on a directed graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Enumeration uses the Bron-Kerbosch algorithm with pivoting, whose worst-case runtime is $O(3^{n/3})$: the Moon-Moser theorem shows a graph on $n$ vertices can have that many maximal cliques, so the bound is tight. In practice most graphs stay far from the worst case and enumeration is fast. Note that *maximal* is a strictly weaker property than *maximum*: a clique is maximal if it cannot be extended by adding any vertex, but a graph may contain multiple maximal cliques of different sizes. Use `max_clique()` when you specifically want the largest one. Undirected graphs only; results come back with each clique's node IDs sorted, but the cliques themselves are in arbitrary order. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle is itself one maximal clique containing all three nodes: ::: {#10eb1c6b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "A") ) cliques = graph.find_cliques() len(cliques) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#2a02fd88 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} len(cliques[0]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: A path graph instead has one clique per edge, since no three nodes are all mutually connected: ::: {#cb5116a3 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B") .add_edge("B", "C") .add_edge("C", "D") ) len(graph.find_cliques()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: A complete graph collapses down to a single clique containing every node: ::: {#ad159d83 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=False) graph.add_full_graph(n=5) cliques = graph.find_cliques() len(cliques), len(cliques[0]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (1, 5) ``` ::: :::
